intro: Two boxes of cereal in different sizes, a map with a scale in the corner, a sale sign with two stickers, a recipe for four when six people are coming to dinner. Each of these is a problem about comparing two amounts that grow together. The tool for every one of them is the ratio, a comparison of two amounts, and its close relatives: the rate, the unit rate, the proportional relationship and the percent.

This unit starts with ratio language and the pictures that make ratios easy to see: ratio tables, double number lines and tape diagrams. Then it turns ratios into unit rates, the price for one ounce or the miles for one hour, so that different deals and different speeds can be compared fairly. From there it moves to relationships where the ratio never changes, the kind that make a straight line through the origin on a graph and an equation of the form y = kx.

The last part of the unit is percent, the ratio everyone in Illinois meets at a cash register: sales tax, tips, discounts, interest on savings, the error in an estimate and the scale on a drawing. By the end you will be able to tell at a glance which box is the better buy, whether a table is proportional, what a 30% discount followed by a 20% discount really costs, and why it is not 50% off.
bigQuestion: How do ratios, rates and percents let us compare amounts fairly and predict what happens when they grow together?

test.q: What is the ratio 12:20 in simplest form?
test.why: The greatest common factor of 12 and 20 is 4: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so 3:5. 6:10 can still be divided by 2.

test.q: Five pounds of potatoes cost $12.50. What is the unit rate in dollars per pound?
test.why: 12.50 ÷ 5 = 2.50 per pound. The 0.40 comes from dividing in the wrong order, 5 ÷ 12.50.

test.q: A class of 63 students is split into two teams in the ratio 4:5. How many students are on the larger team?
test.why: There are 4 + 5 = 9 boxes, each holding 63 ÷ 9 = 7 students. The larger team has 5 × 7 = 35, and the smaller has 28.

test.q: A car goes 300 miles in 5 hours. At that speed, how far does it go in 8 hours?
test.why: The speed is 300 ÷ 5 = 60 miles per hour, and 8 × 60 = 480 miles.

test.q: How many inches are in 3 yards?
test.why: A yard is 36 inches, so 3 × 36 = 108 inches. Or 3 yards is 9 feet, and 9 × 12 = 108.

test.q: Which table shows a proportional relationship?
test.why: Only in the first table is y ÷ x always the same: 3 ÷ 1 = 3, 6 ÷ 2 = 3, 12 ÷ 4 = 3. The last table gives y = 3 when x = 0, so it cannot be proportional.

test.q: A relationship follows y = 2.5x. What is x when y = 40?
test.why: Solve 40 = 2.5x by dividing: 40 ÷ 2.5 = 16. Check: 2.5 × 16 = 40. The 100 comes from multiplying instead.

test.q: A player made 36 of 45 free throws. What percent did she make?
test.why: 36 ÷ 45 = 0.80, which is 80%. Both numbers divide by 9 to give 4/5, and 4/5 is 80%.

test.q: A store's weekly sales drop from 60 items to 45 items. What is the percent decrease?
test.why: The change is 15, and 15 ÷ 60 = 0.25, so 25%. Dividing by the new amount, 15 ÷ 45, gives the wrong 33%.

test.q: A $45 meal gets a 20% tip. What is the total paid?
test.why: 20% of 45 is 0.20 × 45 = 9, and 45 + 9 = 54. The $9 is only the tip, and $36 subtracts it instead of adding.

test.q: How much simple interest does $1,500 earn at 4% per year for 2 years?
test.why: 1,500 × 0.04 × 2 = 120. One year earns $60, so two years earn $120. The $1,620 is the total, not the interest.

test.q: A floor plan uses the scale 1 inch to 8 feet. A room is 2.5 inches long on the plan. How long is the real room?
test.why: 2.5 × 8 = 20 feet. Two inches is 16 feet, and the extra half inch is 4 feet more.

test.q: A $50 game is 10% off, then an extra 10% off the sale price. What is the final price?
test.why: 50 × 0.90 = 45, then 45 × 0.90 = 40.50. The two discounts multiply to 0.81, a 19% discount, not 20%.

test.q: Bagels sell 6 for $4.50 or 10 for $7.00. Which is the better deal?
choices: 6 for $4.50, because it costs less in total
test.why: 4.50 ÷ 6 = $0.75 per bagel and 7.00 ÷ 10 = $0.70 per bagel, so the 10-pack costs less for each bagel.

write.prompt: Two stores sell the same jeans. Store A lists them at $60 with 25% off. Store B lists them at $52 with 10% off. Both stores add 8% sales tax to the sale price. Find the total cost at each store, decide which is cheaper, and explain each step so a classmate could follow it.
tips: State your final answer first: which store is cheaper and by how much.
Show each percent step with the actual numbers, such as 0.25 × 60 = 15.
Say why you take the discount before the tax and what multiplier each step uses.
Check your work a second way, such as multiplying by 0.75 and 1.08 in one line.
Use dollars and cents in every amount, rounded to the nearest cent.

title: Ratios, Rates and Proportions

chapters.title: Ratios and Unit Rates
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a ratio let you compare two things fairly when they come in different amounts?

story.title: Two Boxes, One Calculator
story.kicker: Maya has six dollars, two boxes of the same cereal and a phone calculator, and she wants to know which box is the better buy.
paragraphs: On a Saturday morning Maya stands in the cereal aisle of a grocery store on the South Side of Chicago. Two boxes of the same cereal sit side by side. The small box holds 12 ounces and costs $3.00. The large box holds 18 ounces and costs $4.20. The large box costs more, but it also holds more. Maya wants to know which box gives more cereal for each dollar. Her brother Theo says the answer is obvious: the big box is always the better deal.

Maya is not sure, so she opens the calculator on her phone. She divides the price of the small box by its size: 3.00 ÷ 12 = 0.25. That means 25 cents for every ounce. Then she does the same for the large box: 4.20 ÷ 18 = 0.2333…, or about 23 cents for every ounce. The large box costs less per ounce. Theo grins. This time he was right.

In the next aisle they find orange juice. A 64-ounce bottle costs $4.80, and a 96-ounce bottle costs $7.68. Theo reaches for the big one. Maya checks first: 4.80 ÷ 64 = 0.075, which is 7.5 cents per ounce. Then 7.68 ÷ 96 = 0.08, which is 8 cents per ounce. This time the small bottle is the better deal. Bigger is not always cheaper. Theo stops grinning.

What Maya did in both aisles was turn a price and a size into a rate for exactly one ounce. A rate for one unit is called a unit rate. It lets you compare things that come in different amounts. The same idea works for a runner's speed and for the water in a recipe. It works for the inches on a map and the miles a car gets from a gallon of gas. This chapter is about ratios, the comparisons behind every one of those.
story.think: Why did dividing each price by the number of ounces let Maya compare boxes of different sizes fairly? What would go wrong if she compared only the two prices?

lessons.title: What a Ratio Compares
lessons.mainIdea: A ratio compares two amounts by telling how many of one there are for each amount of the other.
reading: A fruit bowl holds 3 apples and 5 oranges. The *ratio* of apples to oranges is 3 to 5. You can write it as 3:5 or as 3/5. A ratio is a comparison of two amounts by how many of each there are. Order matters. The ratio of apples to oranges is 3:5, but the ratio of oranges to apples is 5:3. Always write the numbers in the same order as the words.

Some ratios compare one part to another part, like apples to oranges. That is a *part-to-part ratio*. Other ratios compare a part to the whole group. The bowl has 3 + 5 = 8 pieces of fruit, so the ratio of apples to all fruit is 3:8. That is a *part-to-whole ratio*. A common mistake is to mix these up. In a class of 12 girls and 15 boys, the ratio of girls to boys is 12:15, but the ratio of girls to students is 12:27, because 12 + 15 = 27.

A ratio does not tell you the actual counts. A ratio of 3:5 could mean 3 apples and 5 oranges, or 30 apples and 50 oranges, or 300 and 500. It only tells you how the two amounts compare. That is why people often say a ratio with the words for every: for every 3 apples there are 5 oranges. If you know the ratio and one real count, you can find the other. With 5 oranges for every 3 apples, 15 oranges means 9 apples.

words.d: a comparison of two amounts, such as 3 apples to 5 oranges, written 3:5 or 3/5
a ratio that compares one part of a group to another part, like girls to boys
a ratio that compares one part of a group to the whole group, like girls to all students

look.title: A Bag of Marbles
look.text: A bag holds 4 red marbles and 6 blue marbles, and nothing else. Write the ratio of red to blue. Then write the ratio of blue to red. Then write the ratio of red marbles to all the marbles in the bag. One of these three ratios is part-to-whole; the other two are part-to-part.
look.prompt: Which of your three ratios is part-to-whole, and what number did you have to add up to write it?

check.q: A team has 7 wins and 4 losses. What is the ratio of wins to losses?
check.why: Wins come first in the words, so wins come first in the ratio: 7 wins to 4 losses is 7:4.

check.q: The same team has 7 wins and 4 losses. What is the ratio of losses to all games played?
check.why: The whole is 7 + 4 = 11 games, so losses to all games is 4:11. 4:7 compares losses to wins, a part-to-part ratio.

check.q: A pet shelter has cats and dogs in the ratio 2:3. Which statement means the same thing?
choices: There are exactly 2 cats and 3 dogs
For every 2 cats there are 3 dogs
For every 3 cats there are 2 dogs
2 out of every 3 animals are cats
check.why: A ratio gives the comparison, not the actual counts, so 2:3 means for every 2 cats there are 3 dogs; there could be 20 cats and 30 dogs.

lessons.title: Equivalent Ratios
lessons.mainIdea: Two ratios are equivalent when you can multiply or divide both parts of one by the same number to get the other.
reading: A lemonade recipe uses 2 cups of lemon juice for 6 cups of water, a ratio of 2:6. To make twice as much, double both amounts: 4 cups of juice for 12 cups of water, 4:12. To make half as much, halve both: 1 cup of juice for 3 cups of water, 1:3. All three batches taste the same, because the mix is the same. Ratios that describe the same comparison are called *equivalent ratios*. You make one by multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number.

The ratio with the smallest whole numbers is the *simplest form*. To find it, divide both parts by their *greatest common factor*, the largest number that divides both. For 12:18, the greatest common factor is 6, so 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3. The simplest form is 2:3. A common mistake is adding the same number to both parts. 2:6 and 3:7 are not equivalent. The first is 1 cup of juice for every 3 cups of water, and the second is much stronger.

To test whether two ratios are equivalent, simplify both and compare. Are 8:20 and 6:15 equivalent? Divide 8:20 by 4 to get 2:5. Divide 6:15 by 3 to get 2:5. They match, so yes. You can also work upward from the simplest form: 2:5 times 4 is 8:20, and 2:5 times 3 is 6:15. Either way, every equivalent ratio comes from the same simplest form.

words.d: ratios that describe the same comparison, like 2:6 and 1:3
the equivalent ratio with the smallest whole numbers, like 2:3 for 12:18
the largest number that divides both numbers evenly; for 12 and 18 it is 6

look.title: Mixing Green Paint
look.text: A painter mixes 3 parts blue paint with 5 parts yellow paint to get a certain green. She has 20 cups of yellow and wants to use all of it. To keep the same green, she needs an equivalent ratio: 5 × 4 = 20, so she multiplies the blue by 4 as well, 3 × 4 = 12 cups of blue. The ratio 12:20 simplifies back to 3:5.
look.prompt: If she had 35 cups of yellow instead, how many cups of blue would keep the same shade of green?

check.q: Which ratio is equivalent to 4:10?
check.why: Divide both parts of 4:10 by 2 to get 2:5. 5:11 adds 1 to each part, and 8:10 and 4:20 change only one part.

check.q: What is the simplest form of the ratio 24:36?
check.why: The greatest common factor of 24 and 36 is 12, so 24 ÷ 12 = 2 and 36 ÷ 12 = 3, giving 2:3. 12:18 and 4:6 can still be divided further.

check.q: A recipe uses 3 eggs for every 2 cups of flour. How many eggs go with 8 cups of flour?
check.why: 8 cups is 2 × 4, so multiply the eggs by 4 too: 3 × 4 = 12 eggs. The ratio 12:8 simplifies to 3:2.

lessons.title: Tape Diagrams for Ratios
lessons.mainIdea: A tape diagram draws each part of a ratio as equal boxes, so you can find the value of one box and then every amount.
reading: A basketball league has boys and girls in the ratio 3:2, and 25 players in all. How many are boys? Draw a *tape diagram*: a strip of 3 equal boxes for boys and a strip of 2 equal boxes for girls. Every box stands for the same number of players. There are 3 + 2 = 5 boxes, and they share 25 players, so each box holds 25 ÷ 5 = 5 players. Boys fill 3 boxes: 3 × 5 = 15. Girls fill 2 boxes: 2 × 5 = 10. Check: 15 + 10 = 25.

Sometimes you know the *difference* instead of the total. A paint mix uses red and blue in the ratio 5:3, and there are 8 more liters of red than blue. Red has 5 boxes and blue has 3, so red has 5 − 3 = 2 more boxes. Those 2 boxes hold the 8 extra liters, so each box holds 8 ÷ 2 = 4 liters. Red is 5 × 4 = 20 liters and blue is 3 × 4 = 12 liters. Check the difference: 20 − 12 = 8.

The most common mistake is dividing the total by one number from the ratio. For the basketball problem, 25 ÷ 3 gives a decimal that means nothing here. The total is shared by all the boxes, so divide by the sum of the ratio parts. The second mistake is stopping after finding the value of one box. Five players per box is not the answer. Multiply back to get the number of boys.

words.d: a drawing of equal boxes in strips, one strip for each part of a ratio
how much more one amount is than another, found by subtracting

look.title: Sharing Fifty-Six Dollars
look.text: Sam and Ana earn $56 together and agree to split it in the ratio 4:3 because Sam worked longer. Draw 4 boxes for Sam and 3 boxes for Ana. That is 7 boxes sharing $56, so each box is worth 56 ÷ 7 = $8. Sam gets 4 × 8 = $32 and Ana gets 3 × 8 = $24. Check: 32 + 24 = 56.
look.prompt: Suppose instead you were told only that Sam got $8 more than Ana. Could you still find each share from the ratio 4:3? Try it.

check.q: A shelter has cats and dogs in the ratio 2:5, with 35 animals in all. How many dogs are there?
check.why: There are 2 + 5 = 7 boxes, so each box is 35 ÷ 7 = 5 animals. Dogs fill 5 boxes: 5 × 5 = 25. The 10 is the number of cats.

check.q: A drink mixes juice and water in the ratio 3:1. There are 12 more cups of juice than water. How many cups are there in all?
check.why: Juice has 3 − 1 = 2 more boxes, so each box is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cups. Juice is 18 cups and water is 6 cups, and 18 + 6 = 24.

check.q: In the boys-to-girls problem with a 3:2 ratio and 25 players, why do you divide 25 by 5?
choices: Because 5 is the bigger number in the ratio
Because 3 + 2 = 5 boxes share the 25 players equally
Because five players are on the court at a time
check.why: The total belongs to all the boxes together, and there are 3 + 2 = 5 boxes, so each box gets 25 ÷ 5 = 5 players.

lessons.title: Ratio Tables
lessons.mainIdea: A ratio table lists equivalent ratios in rows, so you can scale a ratio up or down to find a missing amount.
reading: A bakery sells 5 muffins for $4. A *ratio table* lists equivalent ratios in rows: 5 muffins for $4, 10 muffins for $8, 15 muffins for $12, 20 muffins for $16. Each row comes from multiplying both numbers in the first row by the same amount. To *scale up*, multiply; to *scale down*, divide. The table makes it easy to see what 20 muffins cost, because you can read the answer straight from the row.

You can also add rows. The row 5 muffins for $4 plus the row 10 muffins for $8 gives 15 muffins for $12, and that row is already in the table. Adding works because every row is the same ratio. To find the cost of 35 muffins, notice that 35 = 5 × 7, so the cost is 4 × 7 = $28. Or add rows: 20 muffins plus 15 muffins is 35 muffins, and $16 plus $12 is $28. Both routes agree.

When the number you want is not a neat multiple, go through 1. Five muffins cost $4, so 1 muffin costs 4 ÷ 5 = $0.80. Then 7 muffins cost 7 × 0.80 = $5.60. The most common mistake with a ratio table is changing one column and not the other. If you double the muffins, you must double the dollars. A row that says 10 muffins for $4 is a different, much cheaper bakery.

words.d: a table whose rows are equivalent ratios, like 5 muffins for $4 and 10 muffins for $8
multiply both parts of a ratio by the same number to get a larger equivalent ratio
divide both parts of a ratio by the same number to get a smaller equivalent ratio

look.title: The Bakery's Price Table
look.cite: Example price table built from the ratio 5 muffins for $4
look.prompt: Every row is 5 muffins for $4 scaled up. Which two rows add to make the 35-muffin row, and what would 45 muffins cost?

check.q: A ratio table starts with 3 pens for $2. What do 18 pens cost?
check.why: 18 pens is 3 × 6, so the cost is 2 × 6 = $12. The answer $6 multiplies only one column, and $36 multiplies by 18 instead of 6.

check.q: A ratio table has the rows 4 → 10 and 8 → 20. Which row also belongs in the table?
check.why: Adding the two rows gives 4 + 8 = 12 and 10 + 20 = 30, so 12 → 30 fits. Each row is the ratio 2:5, and 12:30 simplifies to 2:5.

check.q: Two bags of soil weigh 7 pounds. How much do 9 bags weigh?
check.why: Go through 1 bag: 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5 pounds per bag, and 9 × 3.5 = 31.5 pounds. 63 comes from multiplying 7 by 9 without dividing by 2.

lessons.title: Double Number Lines
lessons.mainIdea: A double number line lines up two amounts that grow together, so equal jumps on one line match equal jumps on the other.
reading: Jada runs 3 miles every 24 minutes. A *double number line* shows this with two number lines, one above the other. The top line counts miles: 0, 3, 6, 9. The bottom line counts minutes: 0, 24, 48, 72. Each *tick mark* on the top line sits directly above its partner on the bottom line. Reading straight down from 6 miles lands on 48 minutes. Both lines start at 0, because 0 miles takes 0 minutes.

To answer a question the lines do not show directly, find the value for 1. Jada takes 24 minutes for 3 miles, so 1 mile takes 24 ÷ 3 = 8 minutes. In 60 minutes she runs 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5 miles. You can see this on the lines too. Sixty minutes sits halfway between 48 and 72. Halfway between their partners, 6 and 9 miles, is 7.5 miles. The picture and the arithmetic agree.

Two mistakes spoil a double number line. The first is uneven spacing. The jumps on each line must be equal, or reading across gives the wrong partner. The second is starting one line at a number other than 0. Both lines must begin at the same 0, because nothing of one amount goes with nothing of the other. A ratio table and a double number line hold the same information, but the line shows the order and the gaps.

words.d: two number lines, one above the other, whose matching tick marks show equivalent ratios
a short line on a number line that marks one value

look.title: Filling a Kiddie Pool
look.text: A hose fills 10 gallons every 4 minutes. Draw a double number line: the top line counts gallons 0, 10, 20, 30, and the bottom line counts minutes 0, 4, 8, 12. To find the time for 25 gallons, notice that 25 sits halfway between 20 and 30, so its time is halfway between 8 and 12 minutes: 10 minutes. Check with the rate: 10 gallons in 4 minutes is 2.5 gallons per minute, and 25 ÷ 2.5 = 10.
look.prompt: How many gallons are in the pool after 18 minutes? Find the answer two ways: on the lines and with the rate.

check.q: A cyclist rides 5 km every 30 minutes. How far does she ride in 90 minutes?
check.why: 90 minutes is 3 jumps of 30 minutes, so the distance is 3 jumps of 5 km: 15 km. The 45 comes from multiplying 5 by 9 instead of by 3.

check.q: On a double number line for miles and minutes, why do both lines share the same 0?
choices: Because every number line has to start at 0
Because zero is the smallest number
Because 0 minutes of running means 0 miles run
Because it makes the drawing look neat
check.why: The two amounts grow together from nothing: at 0 minutes, 0 miles have been run, so the two zeros are partners.

check.q: A double number line shows pounds of apples 0, 3, 6, 9 above dollars 0, 4, 8, 12. What do 7.5 pounds cost?
check.why: 7.5 pounds is halfway between 6 and 9, so the cost is halfway between $8 and $12, which is $10. Check: 3 pounds cost $4, so 7.5 pounds cost 2.5 × 4 = $10.

lessons.title: Finding a Unit Rate
lessons.mainIdea: A unit rate tells how much of one amount goes with exactly 1 of the other, and you find it by dividing.
reading: A *rate* is a ratio of two amounts with different units, like miles and hours or dollars and pounds. A car drives 240 miles in 4 hours. To find how far it goes in 1 hour, divide: 240 ÷ 4 = 60 miles per hour. A rate for exactly 1 of the second amount is a *unit rate*. The word *per* means for each 1. Sixty miles per hour means 60 miles for each 1 hour.

At the store, 3 pounds of apples cost $5.40. The unit rate is 5.40 ÷ 3 = $1.80 per pound. Every ratio actually has two unit rates. You could also divide the other way: 3 ÷ 5.40 = 0.555…, about 0.56 pounds per dollar. Both are true. Pick the one that answers the question. To compare prices, dollars per pound is the useful one. To see how much a dollar buys, pounds per dollar is.

The common mistake is dividing in the wrong order. For the car, 4 ÷ 240 = 0.0167 hours per mile is a real rate, but it is not miles per hour. The amount before per goes on top and the amount after per is the 1 you divide by. This is exactly what Maya did in the cereal aisle: $3.00 ÷ 12 ounces = $0.25 per ounce. Price first, then divide by the number of ounces.

words.d: a ratio of two amounts with different units, like 240 miles in 4 hours
a rate with 1 as the second amount, like 60 miles per 1 hour or $1.80 per 1 pound
for each 1; 60 miles per hour means 60 miles for each 1 hour

look.title: Miles for Each Gallon
look.text: A car goes 150 miles on 5 gallons of gas. The unit rate is 150 ÷ 5 = 30 miles per gallon. With 8 gallons in the tank, the car can go 8 × 30 = 240 miles. The other unit rate, 5 ÷ 150 = 0.033 gallons per mile, is true too, but miles per gallon is the one drivers use.
look.prompt: A second car goes 200 miles on 8 gallons. Find its miles per gallon. Which car goes farther on one gallon?

check.q: Twelve oranges cost $3.60. What is the unit rate in dollars per orange?
check.why: 3.60 ÷ 12 = 0.30, so each orange costs $0.30. The $3.33 comes from dividing in the wrong order, 12 ÷ 3.60.

check.q: A train covers 420 miles in 6 hours. What is its speed in miles per hour?
check.why: 420 ÷ 6 = 70 miles per hour. Check: 6 × 70 = 420.

check.q: Which of these is a unit rate?
check.why: A unit rate has 1 as its second amount. $2.50 per pound means $2.50 for each 1 pound; the others compare amounts that are not 1.

lessons.title: Comparing Rates: the Better Deal
lessons.mainIdea: To compare two deals, find each one's unit rate in the same unit and then compare the numbers.
reading: Back to Maya's cereal. The small box is 12 ounces for $3.00: 3.00 ÷ 12 = $0.25 per ounce. The large box is 18 ounces for $4.20: 4.20 ÷ 18 = 0.2333…, about $0.23 per ounce. Now both prices are for the same amount, 1 ounce, so you can *compare* them directly. The large box costs less per ounce, so it is the *better deal*. Two rates can only be compared when they are in the same units.

The juice showed that bigger is not always cheaper. The 64-ounce bottle for $4.80 is 4.80 ÷ 64 = $0.075 per ounce. The 96-ounce bottle for $7.68 is 7.68 ÷ 96 = $0.08 per ounce. The small bottle wins. A common mistake is to compare the totals, $4.80 and $7.68, and call the cheaper one the better deal. Totals do not tell you the deal, because the bottles hold different amounts.

Rates also compare speeds, and there the bigger number wins. Jo runs 100 meters in 16 seconds: 100 ÷ 16 = 6.25 meters per second. Kim runs 200 meters in 34 seconds: 200 ÷ 34 = 5.88 meters per second. Jo is faster, even though Kim ran farther. So read what the rate measures before you decide. For a price per ounce, smaller is better. For meters per second, bigger is better.

words.d: the choice with the lower price for each unit, like the lower cost per ounce
to look at two amounts in the same unit and decide which is larger, smaller or the same

look.title: Maya's Four Prices per Ounce
look.cite: Example prices from the chapter story, each price divided by its ounces
look.prompt: Which cereal and which juice are the better deals? Why can you compare the two cereals to each other but not a cereal to a juice?

check.q: Rice costs $6.50 for a 5-pound bag or $9.60 for an 8-pound bag. Which is the better deal?
choices: The 5-pound bag, because it costs less in total
They cost the same per pound
check.why: 6.50 ÷ 5 = $1.30 per pound and 9.60 ÷ 8 = $1.20 per pound, so the 8-pound bag costs less for each pound.

check.q: Runner A goes 400 meters in 80 seconds. Runner B goes 300 meters in 50 seconds. Who is faster?
choices: Runner A, because 400 is more than 300
Runner B, because 50 seconds is less than 80
Runner A, at 5 meters per second
Runner B, at 6 meters per second
check.why: 400 ÷ 80 = 5 meters per second and 300 ÷ 50 = 6 meters per second. Runner B covers more ground each second, so B is faster.

check.q: Why can the total price alone not tell you which cereal box is the better deal?
choices: Because the boxes hold different amounts, so you need the price per ounce
Because the larger box is always cheaper
Because a calculator rounds the answer
check.why: The boxes are different sizes, so a fair comparison needs the price for the same amount, 1 ounce, which is the unit rate.

lessons.title: Using a Unit Rate to Predict
lessons.mainIdea: Once you know a unit rate, multiply it by any amount to predict the matching amount, or divide to go backward.
reading: A tutor earns $45 for 3 hours of work. The unit rate is 45 ÷ 3 = $15 per hour. Now you can *predict* pay for any number of hours. For 7 hours: 7 × 15 = $105. You can also go backward. If the tutor earned $120, divide by the unit rate: 120 ÷ 15 = 8 hours. The unit rate is the bridge between the two amounts in both directions.

*Speed* works the same way. Driving from Chicago to Springfield is a trip of about 200 miles. At 60 miles per hour, the time is 200 ÷ 60 = 3.33… hours, about 3 hours and 20 minutes, because 0.33 of an hour is 20 minutes. If you know the time instead, multiply. Two and a half hours at 60 miles per hour covers 2.5 × 60 = 150 miles.

The common mistake is multiplying when you should divide, or the reverse. Ask yourself: am I finding the total, or the number of units? Finding a total from a number of units means multiply. Finding the number of units from a total means divide. The units on the numbers help: $15 per hour × 7 hours = $105, and the hours cancel. $120 ÷ $15 per hour = 8 hours, and the dollars cancel.

words.d: use a rate to figure out an amount you have not measured yet
a rate of distance per unit of time, like 60 miles per hour

look.title: The Office Printer
look.text: A printer prints 24 pages in 3 minutes. The unit rate is 24 ÷ 3 = 8 pages per minute. A 200-page report takes 200 ÷ 8 = 25 minutes. In 12 minutes, the printer produces 12 × 8 = 96 pages. Notice which direction each question goes: minutes from pages means divide, pages from minutes means multiply.
look.prompt: A second printer prints 30 pages in 4 minutes. How long does the 200-page report take on it? Which printer is faster?

check.q: A tutor earns $15 per hour. How much does she earn for 6.5 hours?
check.why: 6.5 × 15 = 97.50. Six hours is $90, and the extra half hour is $7.50.

check.q: A bus travels at 55 miles per hour. How long does a 220-mile trip take?
check.why: 220 ÷ 55 = 4 hours. Check: 4 × 55 = 220. The 12,100 comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

check.q: A leaky faucet drips 2 liters every 5 hours. How much water drips in 24 hours?
check.why: The unit rate is 2 ÷ 5 = 0.4 liters per hour, and 24 × 0.4 = 9.6 liters. The 60 comes from multiplying 24 by 2.5, the hours per liter.

lessons.title: Converting Units With Rates
lessons.mainIdea: A unit conversion is a rate like 12 inches per 1 foot, so you multiply or divide by it just like any other rate.
reading: There are 12 inches in 1 foot. That is a rate, 12 inches per foot, and using it is a *unit conversion*. To change 5.5 feet to inches, multiply: 5.5 × 12 = 66 inches. To change 90 inches to feet, divide: 90 ÷ 12 = 7.5 feet. The number 12 is the *conversion factor*, the unit rate between the two units. Every conversion works the same way: multiply to get the smaller unit, divide to get the larger one.

The metric system uses conversion factors that are powers of 10. There are 1,000 meters in a kilometer, 1,000 grams in a kilogram and 100 centimeters in a meter. So 3.2 kilometers is 3.2 × 1,000 = 3,200 meters, and 450 grams is 450 ÷ 1,000 = 0.45 kilograms. The ratio of meters to kilometers is 1,000:1, and every metric conversion is a ratio like that.

Some conversions take two steps. A speed of 30 miles per hour in miles per minute: 1 hour is 60 minutes, so 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 miles per minute. A well-known result: 60 miles per hour is 88 feet per second, because 60 × 5,280 feet ÷ 3,600 seconds = 88. The common mistake is multiplying when you should divide. Check with sense: converting to a smaller unit gives a bigger number, since it takes more inches than feet to measure the same wall.

words.d: changing a measurement from one unit to another, like feet to inches
the unit rate between two units, like 12 inches per foot or 1,000 meters per kilometer

look.title: U.S. Length Units
look.prompt: How many inches are in 2.5 yards? How many yards are in 2 miles? Say for each whether you multiplied or divided.

check.q: How many inches are in 4.25 feet?
check.why: 4.25 × 12 = 51. Four feet is 48 inches, and a quarter foot is 3 more inches.

check.q: A bag of flour weighs 2,500 grams. How many kilograms is that?
check.why: There are 1,000 grams in a kilogram, so 2,500 ÷ 1,000 = 2.5 kg. Going to a larger unit gives a smaller number.

check.q: A car travels 45 miles per hour. What is that in miles per minute?
check.why: An hour is 60 minutes, so 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75 miles per minute. The 2,700 comes from multiplying by 60 instead of dividing.

lessons.title: Recipes, Maps and Speeds
lessons.mainIdea: Recipes, map scales and speeds are all ratios, so the same tools of scaling, tables and unit rates solve all of them.
reading: A rice recipe for 4 servings uses 3 cups of rice. You need 10 servings. Find the rate per *serving*: 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75 cups per serving. Then 10 × 0.75 = 7.5 cups. A ratio table gets there too: 4 servings use 3 cups, 8 servings use 6 cups, 2 servings use 1.5 cups, so 10 servings use 6 + 1.5 = 7.5 cups. Both methods agree.

A map's *scale* is a ratio between a length on the map and the real distance. Suppose a map says 1 inch stands for 25 miles. Two cities 3.5 inches apart on the map are 3.5 × 25 = 87.5 miles apart. Going backward, a real distance of 200 miles, about the drive from Chicago to Springfield, is 200 ÷ 25 = 8 inches on that map. The scale is a unit rate: 25 miles per inch.

Speed is a rate of distance per time. A cyclist rides 18 miles in 1.5 hours, so her speed is 18 ÷ 1.5 = 12 miles per hour. A 30-mile ride at that speed takes 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5 hours. The common mistake is mixing minutes and hours. If the ride took 90 minutes, convert first: 90 minutes is 1.5 hours. Dividing 18 by 90 gives miles per minute, a different rate, and comparing it with miles per hour is meaningless.

words.d: the ratio between a length on a map or drawing and the real length it stands for
one portion of a recipe; recipes list amounts for a set number of servings

look.title: Reading a Trail Map
look.text: A trail map uses the scale 1 cm to 4 km. Two campsites are 6.5 cm apart on the map. Their real distance is 6.5 × 4 = 26 km. A hiker walks 4 km per hour, so the walk takes 26 ÷ 4 = 6.5 hours. Both the map scale and the walking speed are unit rates, and each one turns one amount into another with a single multiplication or division.
look.prompt: A lake on the same map is 2.25 cm from the first campsite. How far is that in kilometers, and how long would the hike take at 4 km per hour?

check.q: A recipe for 6 servings uses 2 cups of beans. How many cups are needed for 15 servings?
check.why: 15 servings is 2.5 times 6 servings, so multiply the beans by 2.5: 2 × 2.5 = 5 cups. Or 2 ÷ 6 = 1/3 cup per serving, and 15 × 1/3 = 5.

check.q: A map uses the scale 1 inch to 40 miles. Two towns are 2.75 inches apart on the map. How far apart are they?
check.why: 2.75 × 40 = 110 miles. Two inches is 80 miles, and 0.75 inch is 30 more miles.

check.q: A car drives 100 miles in 2.5 hours. At the same speed, how long does a 140-mile trip take?
check.why: The speed is 100 ÷ 2.5 = 40 miles per hour, and 140 ÷ 40 = 3.5 hours. Check: 3.5 × 40 = 140.

review.q: A box holds 9 red pens and 6 blue pens. What is the ratio of red to blue in simplest form?
review.why: Divide both parts of 9:6 by their greatest common factor, 3: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 and 6 ÷ 3 = 2, so 3:2. Red comes first.

review.q: Eight pencils cost $2. Using a ratio table, what do 20 pencils cost?
review.why: 20 pencils is 2.5 times 8 pencils, so the cost is 2.5 × 2 = $5. Or 1 pencil costs $0.25 and 20 × 0.25 = 5.

review.q: A car goes 210 miles in 3.5 hours. What is its speed?
review.why: 210 ÷ 3.5 = 60 miles per hour. Check: 3.5 × 60 = 210. The 735 comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

review.q: Forty students are split into two groups in the ratio 3:5. How many students are in the smaller group?
review.why: There are 3 + 5 = 8 boxes, each holding 40 ÷ 8 = 5 students. The smaller group has 3 × 5 = 15 students, and the larger has 25.

review.q: Apples sell 3 for $2.40 or 5 for $3.75. Which is the better deal?
choices: 3 for $2.40, because it costs less in total
review.why: 2.40 ÷ 3 = $0.80 per apple and 3.75 ÷ 5 = $0.75 per apple, so the 5-pack costs less for each apple.

review.q: How many inches are in 7 yards?
review.why: A yard is 36 inches, so 7 × 36 = 252 inches. The 84 comes from using 12 inches per yard, and 21 is the number of feet.

review.q: A double number line shows hours 0, 2, 4, 6 above miles 0, 90, 180, 270. How many miles go with 5 hours?
review.why: Two hours is 90 miles, so 1 hour is 45 miles and 5 hours is 5 × 45 = 225 miles. It sits halfway between 180 and 270.
Both 6:9 and 4:6 simplify to 2:3: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, 9 ÷ 3 = 3, and 4 ÷ 2 = 2, 6 ÷ 2 = 3. 8:11 adds 2 to each part, which changes the ratio.

chapters.title: Proportional Relationships and Percent
chapters.bigQuestion: When two amounts grow together, how can you tell whether they stay in the same ratio, and what does a percent tell you about that ratio?

story.title: Thirty Percent Off, Then Twenty More
story.kicker: A jacket, two sale stickers and an argument at the register: is 30% off followed by 20% off the same as 50% off?
paragraphs: Devon finds the jacket he has wanted all fall on a rack near the front of a store on State Street. The tag says $80. A sign above the rack says 30% off. Then he spots a smaller sticker on the tag: take an extra 20% off all sale prices. Devon does the math in his head. Thirty plus twenty is fifty. Half off. The jacket is forty dollars. He carries it to the register before anyone can change their mind. His sister Lena follows him, frowning. She is not so sure the math works that way.

The cashier scans the tag. The register takes 30% off first: 30% of $80 is 0.30 × 80 = $24, so the price drops to $56. Then it takes 20% off that: 20% of $56 is 0.20 × 56 = $11.20, so the price drops to $44.80. Devon stares at the screen. Forty-four eighty is not forty. Did the store cheat him? The cashier shakes her head. The second discount comes off the sale price, she says, not the original price. Twenty percent of a smaller number is a smaller number.

On the walk home Lena works it out another way. After 30% off, you pay 70% of the price: 0.70 × 80 = 56. After another 20% off, you pay 80% of that: 0.80 × 56 = 44.80. Multiply the two: 0.70 × 0.80 = 0.56, so Devon paid 56% of the original price. That is 44% off, not 50%. No matter what the price is, two discounts of 30% and 20% will never add up to 50%. Devon admits she is right. He still likes the jacket.

A percent is a ratio with 100 as its second number. Ratios do not add the way Devon expected. This chapter is about relationships where two amounts stay in the same ratio as they grow. They are called proportional relationships. It is also about percent, the most common way people describe those ratios. You will learn to spot a proportional relationship in a table, a graph or an equation. You will handle tax, tips, discounts, interest, errors and scale drawings with confidence.
story.think: Why is 30% off followed by 20% off less than 50% off? What would the second sticker have to say for the jacket to really cost $40?

lessons.title: Spotting a Proportional Table
lessons.mainIdea: A relationship is proportional when every pair in its table has the same ratio, so dividing y by x always gives the same number.
reading: A bike rental shop charges $6 per hour. One hour costs $6, 2 hours cost $12, 3 hours cost $18 and 5 hours cost $30. Divide the cost by the hours in each row: 6 ÷ 1 = 6, 12 ÷ 2 = 6, 18 ÷ 3 = 6, 30 ÷ 5 = 6. The answer is always 6. When two amounts always have the same ratio like this, they are in a *proportional relationship*. The number that stays the same, here 6, is a *constant*.

A second shop charges a $10 fee plus $4 per hour. One hour costs $14, 2 hours cost $18 and 3 hours cost $22. Divide again: 14 ÷ 1 = 14, but 18 ÷ 2 = 9, and 22 ÷ 3 = 7.33…. The ratio changes, so this relationship is not proportional. There is another giveaway. In a proportional relationship, 0 of one amount goes with 0 of the other. Renting for 0 hours at the first shop costs $0, but at the second shop it still costs the $10 fee.

The test is simple: divide y by x in every row and see whether you always get the same number. A common mistake is checking only whether y goes up by the same amount each time. The second shop's costs go up by 4 each hour, 14, 18, 22, and that steady climb looks proportional, but it is not, because the ratio y ÷ x keeps changing. Equal steps are not enough. The ratio must be equal in every row.

words.d: a relationship between two amounts in which every pair has the same ratio, like cost and hours at $6 per hour
a number that stays the same, like the 6 in a table where y ÷ x is always 6

look.title: Bike Rental at $6 per Hour
look.cite: Example bike rental with no fee, charging $6 per hour
look.prompt: Divide the dollars by the hours in each row. What do you get every time? What would the table look like if the shop added a $10 fee?

check.q: Which table shows a proportional relationship?
check.why: Only in the first table is y ÷ x the same in every row: 5 ÷ 1 = 5, 10 ÷ 2 = 5, 15 ÷ 3 = 5. In the second table, 5 ÷ 1 = 5 but 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5.

check.q: A table has the rows x = 2, y = 9; x = 4, y = 18; x = 6, y = 27. Is it proportional?
choices: No, because y does not go up by the same amount
Yes, because y ÷ x is 4.5 in every row
No, because 9 is not a multiple of 2
Yes, because y goes up by 9 each time
check.why: 9 ÷ 2 = 4.5, 18 ÷ 4 = 4.5 and 27 ÷ 6 = 4.5, so the ratio is the same in every row. Equal steps alone would not prove it.

check.q: Which point must every proportional relationship include?
check.why: In a proportional relationship, 0 of one amount goes with 0 of the other, so the pair (0, 0) is always included.

lessons.title: The Constant of Proportionality
lessons.mainIdea: In a proportional relationship y = kx, the constant k is the unit rate, and it tells you what y is when x is 1.
reading: At the $6-per-hour bike shop, the cost y for x hours is y = 6 × x, written y = 6x. The number 6 is the *constant of proportionality*, usually called k. It is the unit rate: the cost for 1 hour. Every proportional relationship has an *equation* of the form y = kx. To find k from any row of a table, divide y by x. If a table shows x = 4 and y = 22, then k = 22 ÷ 4 = 5.5, and the equation is y = 5.5x.

Once you have the equation, you can find any pair. With y = 5.5x, when x = 12, y = 5.5 × 12 = 66. Going backward, when y = 99, solve 99 = 5.5x by dividing: x = 99 ÷ 5.5 = 18. Check: 5.5 × 18 = 99. The equation replaces a whole table.

Three T-shirts cost $27. Find the unit rate: 27 ÷ 3 = 9, so k = 9 and y = 9x. Eleven shirts cost 9 × 11 = $99. The common mistake is writing y = x + 9, adding instead of multiplying. Test it with 2 shirts. The table says 2 shirts cost 9 × 2 = $18. The wrong equation gives 2 + 9 = 11, which is not what the store charges.

words.d: the number k in y = kx; it is the unit rate, the value of y when x is 1
a math sentence with an equals sign, like y = 6x, that shows how two amounts are related

look.title: Filling a Swimming Pool
look.text: A pump puts 250 gallons into a pool every 10 minutes. The constant of proportionality is 250 ÷ 10 = 25 gallons per minute, so the equation is y = 25x, where x is minutes and y is gallons. In 45 minutes the pump adds 25 × 45 = 1,125 gallons. To reach 3,000 gallons takes 3,000 ÷ 25 = 120 minutes, which is 2 hours.
look.prompt: Write the equation for a slower pump that puts 180 gallons into the pool every 12 minutes. How long does it take that pump to reach 3,000 gallons?

check.q: In a proportional relationship, x = 5 goes with y = 40. What is the constant of proportionality?
check.why: k = y ÷ x = 40 ÷ 5 = 8. The 35 comes from subtracting and the 200 from multiplying.

check.q: A relationship follows y = 4.5x. What is y when x = 6?
check.why: y = 4.5 × 6 = 27. Four times 6 is 24, and half of 6 is 3 more, so 27. The 10.5 comes from adding instead of multiplying.

check.q: A table shows x = 2, y = 15 and x = 4, y = 30. Which equation fits it?
check.why: k = 15 ÷ 2 = 7.5, and 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5 too, so y = 7.5x. The equation y = 15x gives 30 when x = 2, which does not match the table.

lessons.title: Graphs of Proportional Relationships
lessons.mainIdea: A proportional relationship graphs as a straight line through the origin, and its steepness is the constant k.
reading: Plot the bike shop's table as points: (0, 0), (1, 6), (2, 12), (3, 18). The points line up on a straight line, and that line passes through the *origin*, the point (0, 0) where the axes cross. Every proportional relationship makes a graph like this: a straight line through the origin. The point where x is 1, here (1, 6), shows the unit rate. Its y-value is the constant of proportionality.

The $10-fee shop makes a straight line too, but it crosses the y-axis at 10, not at 0, so it is not proportional. A curve is not proportional either, even if it starts at the origin. Reading a graph runs backward as well. If a cost graph goes through the point (4, 30), then 4 hours cost $30, and k = 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5. From one point you can write the whole equation, y = 7.5x.

Two proportional graphs on the same axes can be compared by *steepness*. The steeper line has the bigger k. A walker's distance line passes through (2, 6), so she walks 6 ÷ 2 = 3 miles per hour. A biker's line passes through (2, 24), so he rides 24 ÷ 2 = 12 miles per hour. The biker's line climbs faster. The common mistake is reading a point in the wrong order. The first number is always x, and the second is always y.

words.d: the point (0, 0) on a graph, where the x-axis and y-axis cross
how quickly a line climbs; in a proportional graph, a steeper line means a larger constant k

look.title: Two Lines Through the Origin
look.text: Line A passes through the origin and the point (3, 12). Line B passes through the origin and the point (5, 15). To compare their constants, divide: for A, 12 ÷ 3 = 4, so y = 4x. For B, 15 ÷ 5 = 3, so y = 3x. Line A is steeper, even though B reaches a higher point in the drawing, because A climbs 4 for every 1 step to the right while B climbs only 3.
look.prompt: A third line goes through (8, 20). Is it steeper than line A, steeper than line B, or between them? Show the division.

check.q: A proportional graph passes through (0, 0) and (5, 35). What is the constant of proportionality?
check.why: k = 35 ÷ 5 = 7, so the equation is y = 7x. Check: 7 × 5 = 35.

check.q: Which graph shows a proportional relationship?
choices: A straight line through (5, 0) that climbs to the right
check.why: A proportional relationship is always a straight line through the origin. A line through (0, 5) has a starting fee, and a curve does not keep a constant ratio.

check.q: On a graph of total cost against number of items, what does the point (6, 45) mean?
check.why: The first number is x, the items, and the second is y, the cost: 6 items cost $45. The unit rate would then be 45 ÷ 6 = $7.50 per item.

lessons.title: Percent Means per Hundred
lessons.mainIdea: A percent is a ratio with 100 as the second number, so 45% means 45 out of every 100.
reading: A *percent* is a ratio whose second number is 100. The word comes from per hundred. Saying 45% means 45 out of every 100, the ratio 45:100, the fraction 45/100 and the decimal 0.45 all at once. Percents make ratios easy to compare because every one is out of the same 100. In a class of 25 students, 20 passed a test. Scale the ratio 20:25 up to 100: multiply both by 4 to get 80:100. So 80% passed.

You will move between fractions, decimals and percents constantly. Fraction to percent: divide, then multiply by 100. For 3/8, 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375, and 0.375 × 100 = 37.5%. Percent to decimal: divide by 100, which moves the decimal point two places left. So 6% is 0.06, not 0.6. That is the most common slip, and it makes every answer ten times too big. Decimal to percent: multiply by 100. So 1.25 is 125%.

Some *benchmark percents* are worth knowing by heart because they come up so often. 50% is 1/2, 25% is 1/4, 20% is 1/5, 10% is 1/10 and 1% is 1/100. 100% is the whole thing. A percent can be larger than 100: if a plant grows from 20 cm to 50 cm, its new height is 250% of the old one, because 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5. Knowing the benchmarks lets you build others: 15% is 10% plus 5%, and 5% is half of 10%.

words.d: a ratio out of 100; 45% means 45 for every 100, or 45/100, or 0.45
a common percent you know as a fraction, like 50% = 1/2 or 25% = 1/4

look.title: Fractions and Their Percents
look.prompt: Using the table, what percent is 3/8? What fraction is 40%? Which rows could you combine to get 35%?

check.q: Eighteen of the 40 students in a club are in seventh grade. What percent is that?
check.why: 18 ÷ 40 = 0.45, which is 45%. Or scale 18:40 up by 2.5 to get 45:100.

check.q: What is 7% written as a decimal?
check.why: Divide by 100: 7 ÷ 100 = 0.07. The decimal point moves two places left, so 0.7 (one place) is ten times too big.

check.q: What is 5/8 as a percent?

lessons.title: Percent of a Number
lessons.mainIdea: To find a percent of a number, change the percent to a decimal or fraction and multiply.
reading: The store took 30% off an $80 jacket. To find 30% of 80, turn the percent into a decimal and multiply: 0.30 × 80 = 24. So the discount was $24. Benchmarks give the same answer another way: 10% of 80 is 8, so 30% is 3 × 8 = 24. Or use the fraction: 30/100 × 80 = 2,400/100 = 24. The percent is the ratio, the *whole* is the number you start with and the *part* is the answer.

The same equation, part = percent × whole, answers three kinds of questions. To find the part: 30% of 80 is 0.30 × 80 = 24. To find the whole: 24 is 30% of what number? Divide: 24 ÷ 0.30 = 80. To find the percent: 24 is what percent of 80? Divide the part by the whole: 24 ÷ 80 = 0.30, which is 30%. Decide which of the three numbers is missing, then multiply or divide to get it.

For mental math, break the percent into benchmarks. For 15% of 60, take 10% of 60, which is 6, and 5% of 60, which is half of that, 3. Add: 6 + 3 = 9. The common mistake is multiplying by the percent number instead of the decimal. 30 × 80 = 2,400 is far too big for 30% of 80. Sanity check every answer: 30% is less than half, so 30% of 80 must be less than 40.

words.d: the full amount that a percent is taken of; in 30% of 80, the whole is 80
the amount a percent gives you; 30% of 80 is the part, 24

look.title: How Students Get to School
look.text: A school has 250 students. Forty percent of them ride the bus. That is 0.40 × 250 = 100 students. Thirty-five students walk. To find what percent walk, divide the part by the whole: 35 ÷ 250 = 0.14, which is 14%. The rest, 250 − 100 − 35 = 115 students, come some other way, and 115 ÷ 250 = 0.46, or 46%. Check: 40 + 14 + 46 = 100.
look.prompt: If 30 students bike to school, what percent is that? Try it with the decimal method and again with benchmarks (10% of 250 is 25).

check.q: What is 25% of 88?
check.why: 25% is 1/4, and 88 ÷ 4 = 22. Or 0.25 × 88 = 22. The 44 is half, which would be 50%.

check.q: Twelve is 40% of what number?
check.why: Whole = part ÷ percent: 12 ÷ 0.40 = 30. Check: 0.40 × 30 = 12. The 4.8 comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

check.q: Which is a correct way to find 15% of 200 in your head?
check.why: 10% of 200 is 20, and 5% is half of that, 10. Adding gives 30. Check: 0.15 × 200 = 30.

lessons.title: Percent Increase and Decrease
lessons.mainIdea: Percent change compares the amount of change to the original amount, never to the new amount.
reading: Rent goes from $800 a month to $880. The change is 880 − 800 = $80. To describe that change as a percent, divide it by the *original amount*: 80 ÷ 800 = 0.10, which is 10%. That is a *percent increase* of 10%. For a *percent decrease*, the same rule applies. A price drops from $50 to $40. The change is 10, and 10 ÷ 50 = 0.20, so the price fell 20%.

The common mistake is dividing by the new amount. For the price drop from 50 to 40, dividing 10 by 40 gives 25%, which is wrong. The percent change always compares the change to where you started. To apply a percent change, find the change and add or subtract it. A 25% increase on $60: 0.25 × 60 = 15, and 60 + 15 = $75. A faster way is one multiplication: a 25% increase means paying 125%, so 1.25 × 60 = 75. A 25% decrease means paying 75%, so 0.75 × 60 = 45.

An increase and a decrease of the same percent do not cancel out. Start with 100, increase by 20% to 120, then decrease by 20%. Twenty percent of 120 is 24, so the result is 96, not 100. The decrease is bigger in dollars because it was taken from a bigger number. This is the same reason Devon's two discounts did not add up: each percent is figured from a different amount.

words.d: the amount something grew, divided by the original amount, written as a percent
the amount something shrank, divided by the original amount, written as a percent
the amount before a change; percent change is always figured from it

look.title: The Season Ticket Price
look.text: A youth league raises its season ticket from $40 to $46. The change is 46 − 40 = $6. Divide by the original: 6 ÷ 40 = 0.15, so the price rose 15%. The next year the league drops it back from $46 to $40. The change is still $6, but now the original is 46, and 6 ÷ 46 = 0.13, about a 13% decrease. The same $6 is a different percent each way.
look.prompt: A bus fare goes from $2.50 to $2.75. What is the percent increase? If it later went back down to $2.50, would the percent decrease be the same number?

check.q: A store's price goes from $20 to $25. What is the percent increase?
check.why: The change is 5, and 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, so 25%. Dividing by the new price, 5 ÷ 25 = 0.20, gives the wrong 20%.

check.q: A $80 coat is marked down 15%. What is the new price?
check.why: 15% of 80 is 0.15 × 80 = 12, and 80 − 12 = 68. Or 0.85 × 80 = 68. The $12 is the discount, not the price.

check.q: Why is percent change figured from the original amount?
choices: Because the new amount is always bigger
Because it gives a smaller number
Because percent change describes how much the original amount changed
check.why: Percent change answers the question of how much the starting amount grew or shrank, so the starting amount is the whole that the change is compared to.

lessons.title: Tax, Tip and Discount
lessons.mainIdea: Tax and tip are percents added to a price, and a discount is a percent taken away, each figured from the price it applies to.
reading: A *discount* is a percent taken off a price. Devon's jacket at $80 with 30% off: 0.30 × 80 = 24 off, so the sale price is 80 − 24 = $56. The one-step way is to multiply by what is left: 100% − 30% = 70%, and 0.70 × 80 = 56. Coupons, sales and student discounts all work like this.

*Sales tax* is a percent added to a price. Tax rates differ from city to city, so suppose a city's rate is 10%. A $40 restaurant meal has 0.10 × 40 = $4 of tax, so the bill is $44. A *tip* is another percent added, usually figured from the price of the food before tax. An 18% tip on the $40 meal is 0.18 × 40 = $7.20. The total paid is 40 + 4 + 7.20 = $51.20. To find a 20% tip fast, take 10% and double it: 10% of 40 is 4, so 20% is 8.

When a discount and a tax both apply, take the discount first, then tax the sale price. The $56 jacket with 8% tax: 0.08 × 56 = 4.48, so the total is 60.48. Or 1.08 × 56 = 60.48. The common mistake is taxing the original $80, which overcharges. And as Devon learned, two discounts in a row are figured one after the other: 80 × 0.70 = 56, then 56 × 0.80 = 44.80. Never add the percents.

words.d: a percent taken off a price, like 30% off an $80 jacket
a percent that a city or state adds to the price of a purchase
a percent of a restaurant bill added as a payment to the server, often 15% to 20%

look.title: Splitting the Pizza Bill
look.text: Four friends order pizza for $24. They leave a 15% tip: 0.15 × 24 = $3.60, so the bill is 24 + 3.60 = $27.60. Split four ways, each pays 27.60 ÷ 4 = $6.90. If they had left a 20% tip instead, the tip would be 0.20 × 24 = $4.80, the bill $28.80 and each share $7.20. One quick way to get 15% is 10% plus half of 10%: 2.40 + 1.20 = 3.60.
look.prompt: Suppose the city adds 8% sales tax to the $24 before the tip. What is the tax, and what does each friend pay with the 15% tip on the food price?

check.q: A $50 shirt is on sale for 20% off. What is the sale price?
check.why: 20% of 50 is 0.20 × 50 = 10, and 50 − 10 = 40. Or 0.80 × 50 = 40. The $10 is the discount, not the price.

check.q: A $60 meal has 8% sales tax added. What is the total?
check.why: 0.08 × 60 = 4.80 of tax, so the total is 60 + 4.80 = $64.80. The $68 adds 8 dollars instead of 8 percent.

check.q: An $80 jacket is 30% off, then an extra 20% off the sale price. What does it cost?
choices: $56, because only the first discount counts
check.why: Take the discounts one at a time: 80 × 0.70 = 56, then 56 × 0.80 = 44.80. The percents do not add to 50.

lessons.title: Simple Interest and Percent Error
lessons.mainIdea: Simple interest is a percent of the starting amount paid for each year, and percent error compares a mistake to the true value.
reading: When you put money in a savings account, the bank pays you *interest*, a percent of your money, for the time it stays there. With *simple interest*, the percent is figured from the starting amount, called the *principal*, every year. The rule is interest = principal × rate × time. Put $500 in an account at 4% per year (an example rate) for 3 years: 500 × 0.04 × 3 = $60. The account then holds 500 + 60 = $560.

Loans work the same way, but you pay the interest. Borrow $1,200 at 6% per year for 2 years: 1,200 × 0.06 × 2 = $144 of interest. You pay back 1,200 + 144 = $1,344. Two common mistakes: forgetting to multiply by the time, and using 6 instead of 0.06. The second one gives 1,200 × 6 × 2 = 14,400, which is more than ten times the loan. A sanity check catches it: 6% of anything is a small slice.

*Percent error* measures how far off a guess or a measurement is. You guess a jar holds 45 jelly beans, and the true count is 50. The error is 50 − 45 = 5. Divide by the true value: 5 ÷ 50 = 0.10, so the percent error is 10%. A ruler reading of 20 cm for a board that is really 25 cm long has an error of 5, and 5 ÷ 25 = 20% error. Always divide by the true value, not the guess, just as percent change always divides by the original.

words.d: interest figured on the starting amount only: principal × rate × time
the starting amount of money saved or borrowed
the difference between a guess and the true value, divided by the true value, as a percent

look.title: Simple Interest on $1,000 at 5%
look.cite: Simple interest on a $1,000 principal at an example rate of 5% per year
look.prompt: Is the interest proportional to the number of years? What is the constant of proportionality, and how does it relate to the 5% rate?

check.q: How much simple interest does $800 earn at 3% per year for 4 years?
check.why: 800 × 0.03 × 4 = 96. One year earns $24, and four years earn 4 × 24 = $96.

check.q: You estimate a box holds 30 marbles. It really holds 40. What is the percent error?
check.why: The error is 40 − 30 = 10, and 10 ÷ 40 = 0.25, so 25%. Dividing by the guess, 10 ÷ 30, gives the wrong 33%.

check.q: When you find percent error, what do you divide the error by?
check.why: Percent error compares the mistake to the true value, so the true value is the whole you divide by.

lessons.title: Scale Drawings
lessons.mainIdea: A scale drawing keeps every length in the same ratio to the real object, so one scale factor converts any drawn length to real life.
reading: A floor plan of an apartment uses the scale 1 inch to 4 feet. Every inch on the paper stands for 4 feet in the real rooms. A bedroom that is 3 inches long on the plan is 3 × 4 = 12 feet long. A drawing like this is a *scale drawing*, and the number that turns paper lengths into real lengths, here 4 feet per inch, is the *scale factor*. It is a constant of proportionality: real length = 4 × drawn length.

Go backward by dividing. A living room 20 feet wide is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 inches wide on the plan. If you redraw the plan at 1 inch to 2 feet, every length on the paper doubles, because each inch now stands for less. The 12-foot bedroom becomes 12 ÷ 2 = 6 inches long. The rooms did not change; only the scale did.

Area does not scale by the same number as length. The bedroom is 3 inches by 2.5 inches on the plan, an area of 7.5 square inches. In real life it is 12 feet by 10 feet, an area of 120 square feet. The lengths grew by 4, but the area grew by 4 × 4 = 16, and 7.5 × 16 = 120. The common mistake is multiplying the area by the scale factor once. When lengths scale by k, areas scale by k × k.

words.d: a drawing in which every length is the real length multiplied by the same ratio, like a map or floor plan
the number that turns a length in a drawing into the real length, like 4 feet per inch

look.title: A Model Car at 1 to 24
look.text: A model car is built at the scale 1:24, so every real length is 24 times the model's length. A real car 168 inches long makes a model 168 ÷ 24 = 7 inches long. If the model is 2.5 inches tall, the real car is 2.5 × 24 = 60 inches tall, which is 5 feet. Going from model to real, multiply by 24; going from real to model, divide by 24.
look.prompt: The real car's wheels are 27 inches across. How big are the model's wheels? Round to the nearest tenth of an inch.

check.q: A map uses the scale 1 inch to 5 feet. A wall is 4.5 inches long on the map. How long is it really?
check.why: 4.5 × 5 = 22.5 feet. Four inches is 20 feet, and the extra half inch is 2.5 feet more.

check.q: A real wall is 30 feet long. On a plan with the scale 1 inch to 6 feet, how long is it drawn?
check.why: Divide by the scale factor: 30 ÷ 6 = 5 inches. The 180 comes from multiplying instead.

check.q: A drawing is enlarged so every length is 3 times as long. How many times as large is the area?
check.why: Area scales by the scale factor squared: 3 × 3 = 9. A 1-by-1 square becomes a 3-by-3 square with area 9.

lessons.title: Percents in a Row
lessons.mainIdea: To apply two percents one after another, multiply by both multipliers in turn; the percents do not simply add.
reading: Every percent change has a *multiplier*: the decimal you multiply by to get the new amount. Thirty percent off means keeping 70%, a multiplier of 0.70. Twenty percent off means a multiplier of 0.80. Devon's jacket: 80 × 0.70 = 56, then 56 × 0.80 = 44.80. Multiply the two multipliers together: 0.70 × 0.80 = 0.56. Devon paid 56% of the original price, so his total discount was 100% − 56% = 44%, not 50%.

*Successive* increases behave the same way. A $200 phone plan rises 10% one year and 10% the next. The multiplier for a 10% increase is 1.10. So 200 × 1.10 = 220, then 220 × 1.10 = 242. The two increases together are 1.10 × 1.10 = 1.21, a 21% rise, not 20%. The second increase was figured on the bigger $220, so it added more dollars than the first.

The order of the multipliers does not matter, because 0.70 × 0.80 and 0.80 × 0.70 are the same number. That is why a discount followed by tax gives the same total as tax followed by the same discount. Devon's $44.80 jacket with 8% sales tax: 44.80 × 1.08 = 48.38, rounded to the cent. The only mistake to avoid is adding the percents. Two discounts of 30% and 20% are never 50% off, and two 10% raises are always a bit more than 20%.

words.d: the decimal you multiply by to apply a percent change, like 0.70 for 30% off or 1.10 for a 10% increase
one after another, like two discounts applied in a row

look.title: Two Stickers on a Pair of Shoes
look.text: A pair of shoes costs $120. One sale takes 25% off, and a second sticker takes 10% off the sale price. The multipliers are 0.75 and 0.90. First: 120 × 0.75 = 90. Second: 90 × 0.90 = 81. The shoes cost $81. A single discount of 35% would give 120 × 0.65 = 78, three dollars less. The two stickers together are 0.75 × 0.90 = 0.675, a discount of 32.5%.
look.prompt: Reverse the order: take 10% off first, then 25% off. Do you get the same $81? Explain why using the multipliers.

check.q: A $100 item is 20% off, then an extra 20% off the sale price. What is the final price?
check.why: 100 × 0.80 = 80, then 80 × 0.80 = 64. The two discounts multiply to 0.64, a total discount of 36%, not 40%.

check.q: What single multiplier applies a 15% discount followed by a 5% sales tax?
check.why: The discount multiplier is 0.85 and the tax multiplier is 1.05, and 0.85 × 1.05 = 0.8925. Subtracting 15 − 5 to get 0.90 is the adding mistake.

check.q: A price rises 10% and then rises 10% again. What is the total percent increase?
check.why: 1.10 × 1.10 = 1.21, so the price is 121% of the original, a 21% increase. Check with $100: 110, then 121.

review.q: In a proportional relationship, x = 3 goes with y = 21. What is the constant of proportionality?

review.why: 0.35 × 60 = 21. With benchmarks: 10% is 6, so 30% is 18, and 5% is 3, giving 18 + 3 = 21.

review.q: A $90 pair of headphones is 15% off. What is the sale price?
A team's wins go from 40 one season to 50 the next. What is the percent increase?
review.why: The change is 10, and 10 ÷ 40 = 0.25, so 25%. Dividing by the new total, 10 ÷ 50, gives the wrong 20%.

review.q: How much simple interest does $2,000 earn at 5% per year for 3 years?
review.why: 2,000 × 0.05 × 3 = 300. One year earns $100, so three years earn $300. The $2,300 is the total in the account, not the interest.

review.q: A map has the scale 1 cm to 50 km. Two cities are 7 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they?
review.why: 7 × 50 = 350 km. The 0.14 comes from dividing instead of multiplying.

review.q: Which equation does NOT show a proportional relationship?
review.why: A proportional relationship has the form y = kx and includes (0, 0). In y = 3x + 1, when x = 0, y = 1, so the ratio y ÷ x is not constant.

review.q: A price is marked 30% off, then 20% off the sale price. What is the total discount from the original price?
review.why: The multipliers are 0.70 × 0.80 = 0.56, so the buyer pays 56% of the original price. That is 100% − 56% = 44% off.
